utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Madam Registrar, good morning to you. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. Yes, I can follow the proceedings in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Oric, and good morning to you. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution. Also good morning to my learned friends of the Defence. I am here together with co-counsel, Ms. Patricia Sellers, Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio, and our acting case manager, Ms. Sanja Bokulic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Wubben, and good morning to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, my learned friends. My name is Vasvija Vidovic. Together with Mr. John Jones I appear for Mr. Naser Oric. With us are our legal assistant, Ms. Jasmina Cosic, and our CaseMap manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Vidovic, and good morning to you and your team. Hopefully, no preliminaries?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Short one, Your Honour. It's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: It is a request for a guidance. I raised it earlier with the Defence. On Monday we sent them a request for a new sequence list, and yesterday I discussed it with lead counsel. She told me that she will try to do her best to update me of the list of the -- to start with after the break by the end of the week, but there might also be a possibility that she's not able to do so but only by the beginning next week. Well, this is a concern of me because we also have to organise and set up scheduling, and this is a strong call and I don't know to what extent the Trial Chamber need this information because I recall for myself that the Prosecution had even to provide a list further -- a very long list, extensive list, a complete list until the end and also try to do its best to provide the Defence with that information. So I would like to call the Defence -- and I know they're doing their best, but beginning next week might be a little bit late. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Wubben. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we are now in a position to expect, after these two witnesses are completed, that we shall re-examine our list of witnesses. The only reason we have not yet submitted it is that we wish to re-examine it. I do understand Mr. Wubben's request, and we will do our best to have this finished before the end of office hours on Friday. However, we wish to wait for the end of the testimony of these two witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I -- okay. I thank you, Madam Vidovic. Please try to do your best. Basically, I don't see that it will be the end of the world if instead of Friday you get it on Monday. So -- anyway, please try to be as practical and cooperative as possible. The other thing is, Katarina, none of our LiveNote monitors are -- LiveNote is not on. The main one, yes, but the other one isn't. So it needs to -- I can do it myself if I knew the password, but I don't know the password. And I think that my two colleagues are in the same position. All right. Thank you. Can we bring the witness in? Are you still hoping to finish with the next witness today?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I can take the next witness very shortly, I think within an hour, an hour and a half. So I would hope so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Jones. Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, within an hour, hour and a half, when such a statement is done, that's promising, I can guarantee because I received yesterday evening an additional list of persons that might be important, but I'll try to do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What do you mean an additional list of persons?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: In addition to the summary, we requested additional information and we gained some --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Wubben. Lieutenant Colonel Dudley, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome back. I see that the representation from the American embassy has changed. Could you please state your names for the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. SCHILDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. My name is Heather Schildge. I'm the deputy legal councillor at the United States embassy.

utterances.speaker: MS. BREECE
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. My name is Yvonne Breece. I am with the department of defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good morning to both of you. Let's continue with the re-examination, and then the witness can leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Good morning from me, Lieutenant Colonel Dudley. Now, yesterday you were shown a lot of documents by the Prosecution and we're going to review them briefly. I don't want you to speculate or make assumptions or try to guess when I show you these documents. If there's something you don't know or aren't able to help with, simply feel free to say so. I'm going to start with P3, which you were shown yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So if the witness could be shown P3. The Bosnian -- also -- yes, if he could see the Bosnian and the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And now first - and it's an obvious point and I won't make it with each document - but this is the 18th of October, 1992, so that's about five months before you arrived in Srebrenica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, looking at this document and looking at the original, can you see anything on it which indicates whether it was either sent or received? Just on the face of the document, whether there's anything which says "received" and a signature or "sent to" and a signature; anything of that nature.

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am looking. This indicates commander's intent, but it doesn't say whether it was sent out or received.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And for this document, you personally can't say whether this is authentic, whether it was actually typed on the 18th of October 1992 or whether it was typed on the 18th of October, 2002.

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. All I have is a photocopy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would you also agree it's not actually addressed to anyone, this order? There isn't actually a specific person or unit to which -- to whom it's addressed.

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it appears to be addressed to the Srebrenica armed forces staff, but again, that's not exactly clear either.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So in fact, on the face of it, there's no indication, is there, of who this would be delivered to if you had this piece of paper in your hand.

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There would be an additional attachment to say who it was going to be distributed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And if a document like this were to be delivered to different units, that would require multiple copies. Correct?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you see any photocopiers when you were in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far -- did I see anything that could produce additional copies of paperwork? The answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And we see at the top there's a reference to the decree law of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Did you ever hear fighters in the enclave referring to decree laws when referring to what they were about?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And in fact you told us that you observed a low level of education among people. I think you said on a couple of occasions - not wishing to be unkind - but they were not much smarter than their animals. Does this document -- what's stated there referring to a decree law of the Presidency, does that tally with what you observed in terms of level of education and training?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as being able to disseminate this information and have it understood and well implemented, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And this document also talks about low units and high units being in constant communication. It refers to a military organisation or establishment structure. You've talked about semi-autonomous village groups, et cetera. Does that fit with what you observed in Srebrenica, that reference to a military organisation of establishment structure or not?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, at the that time I was there, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now if the witness could be shown P7.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And again, I don't want to belabour the point with these documents, but if you could confirm for each one I show, firstly whether there's anything on the face of it which indicates that it was either sent or received.

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm going to pick up the original so I can look at it real quickly and then I'll put it back. No, there's no distribution plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And again, in terms of whether this is authentic or whether it was typed up ten years later, that's not something you can help us with, is it?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing I can say on this one is it's been typed on a typewriter, not a computer or word processor, therefore it would fit into that time frame; however, I cannot confirm or deny that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Then again, if you wanted to suggest that something had been typed in 1992, you'd be more likely to do it on a typewriter than on a computer, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: As far as the codes which are referred to here, did you ever hear of codes being given to any of these semi-autonomous village groups that you referred to while you were in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not, nor did I see the process in action.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When we look at some of what's referred to here, a signals platoon, a mortar company, an AA defence battery, an engineering platoon, an armoured platoon, did the forces that you see in Srebrenica have any of those things? Did they have armoured personnel carries or operational tanks or mortars or anti-aircraft batteries?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is any heavy equipment I saw was inoperable because it either lacked ammunition, fuel, repair parts, or something else. Every piece of equipment was in some state of disrepair and nonfunctional.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones and Lieutenant Colonel Dudley, please allow a pause because we have already missed a segment of one answer. So please try to cooperate as much as you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So in that respect, these references to a mortar company, et cetera, would that seem anomalous in terms of what you observed in March, 1993?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yesterday you said that codes make for quick and efficient communication. You still need a way of actually transmitting, of communicating, would you not, even if you devised a system of codes?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you told us that when you were in Srebrenica in March 1993, communications were "virtually non-existent" were your words. Correct?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So in that case, codes wouldn't actually be of much help.

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: In your question I can't confirm or deny that, based on the operations on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. If we could move on to P10, please. Now, the Prosecution showed you this document yesterday, and it's dated 20 October, 1992. Are you familiar with any of the events or the persons described in this document?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing I can identify on this document is that most of these individuals have Muslim names of some sort; otherwise, I have no idea what this group pass is all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Again, are you able to say or not whether this is authentic or whether this was -- whether this was forged or another way inauthentic?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looking at the photocopies, there's no way that I can confirm or deny that it was authentic or not authentic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I think you told us that Srebrenica was under siege when you were there. Correct?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a very appropriate term, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And as far as you know, was the situation any different in October 1992?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a slightly better condition, but the enclave was still basically surrounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And given that, was there in fact -- was the area between Srebrenica and Tuzla actually controlled by Muslims, by Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't use the term "controlled," but I would use the term that they had some freedom of movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I meant by controlled in such a way that it would be necessary or appropriate to issue passes for people to go to Tuzla and back.

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, I'm going to rephrase that question. Whether you have to pass through enemy territory or not, issuing passes to one group to pass into another enclave would be an appropriate move because that would give them authorisation to be -- to move to the other enclaves so the receiving side would know that they were there for official business.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you ever see any passes when you were in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If the witness could please be shown P20 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, this is the document which is actually from the time frame when you were in Srebrenica; 24 March 1993. It refers to Kutlici unit. Now, first of all, do you know where Kutlici is or are you familiar with any of the -- are you familiar with that location?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I am not. I don't recognise that name and specifically it would have to be shown to me on a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And again, can you see anything on this document which indicates whether it was sent or received?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And are you able to confirm whether or not this is authentic or whether it was typed up at some other time?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no way I can confirm it, looking at this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, just in terms of the format of this document, an authorisation to a unit to mobilise the entire population temporarily housed in a village, does it seem strange or normal to you that it's not addressed to anyone, to any person, and it's not apparent to whom it would be taken?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: My only comment on this one is Kutlici unit is who it's addressed to, obviously in the first paragraph, first sentence. However, how he's going to execute this is very unclear, looking at the situation that was on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And are you, in fact, able to confirm anything about this document; whether it reflects any true facts or events?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Actually, it looks like whoever was going to receive this directive would probably be unable to carry it out because of the situation on the ground at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it I have to take your answer within the context of what you had stated previously, namely, that you don't even know where Kutlici is. So you wouldn't be able to know what the situation on the ground was in Kutlici at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's a very good point. I would assume it was inside the Srebrenica pocket, but unless I was shown that on a map, I cannot confirm or deny it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And if the witness could now be shown P178, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Again, this is a document which you were shown by the Prosecution. It's dated the 15th of October, 1992. I think you recognised Potocari, but apart from Potocari, do you recognise any of the other places mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: With a quick glance, negative.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think what you did say is that, yes, in Potocari when you were in Srebrenica in March 1993, that was on the front line. You also told us the enclave was shrinking. Are you able to say definitely one way or the other whether the front line was in Potocari in October 1992?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot because I didn't have a trace of the front line at that time as a historical reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And again on this document, is there anything on the face of it which shows that it was either sent or received?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Negative.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And again, you can't see, can you, to whom it would be sent?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot -- let me revise my last statement, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually orders are sent to a subordinate unit and then a copy is kept on file with a higher unit. However, neither one of these are indicated on this sheet of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, if you look at line 4, there's a reference to a place called Tegare. Would you understand from this document on the face of it that Tegare is meant to be in free territory, that is in Muslim hands, as of the 15th of October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm looking at number 4, Tegare. I would have no clue.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But from the face of the document, that's what it appears to be stating, that Tegare is on Muslim lines. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Defence Exhibit D966. In fact, Your Honour, I think in the interests of time and the answer given by the witness about this document, it's not necessary for me to proceed with that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, yes, actually, sorry -- I'll revise that. Yes, D966, but there is another document which I was going to review which is not necessary. So, yes, please, D966.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We can take this quickly. This is dated 14th September, 1992, Milici, operator Borivoje Lalovic, and it's the Birac Brigade command. It says at the bottom, "Tegare completely liberated." Are you familiar with whether it would refer to the Serbs or the Muslims on this document with Milici, Birac Brigade command, and the name Borivoje Lalovic?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That appears to be a Serb document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And according to that, Tegare was liberated. Would you understand from that that it was in Serb hands, certainly as of the 14th of September, 1992?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now -- yes, I think in fact that completes the review of documents. There are just a couple of videos, again which you were shown yesterday by the Prosecution. First P427. I think we're going to go to 37.55.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, firstly, we see there, do we not, that that's a UNHCR vehicle?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rather obviously, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And if we play on a bit further.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If we pause there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That man in the blue beret would appear to be with which organisation?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would be an UNPROFOR soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We'll carry on a bit further.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you recall you were shown this yesterday?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Freeze there for a moment. The man with the blue hat, speaking on the telephone, what affiliation would you say he is?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say he is associated with the UN in some capacity. Obviously not an UNPROFOR soldier, probably a UNHCR representative.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you were shown this yesterday -- and perhaps we'll continue a bit further so we can see the satellite dish. [Videotape played].

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If we stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can you see the emblem on his hat?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. It looks like a United Nations maybe UNICEF-type symbol.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We'll carry on a bit further.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I don't know if it was being suggested to you by the Prosecution that maybe that satellite dish belonged to the Bosnians rather than the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the UN using these heavier satellite dishes now as semi-transportable. They were not man-packable, but they were transportable, and they usually had to set up a small generator sometimes to operate them; otherwise, they would be powered out of the vehicle. That satellite dish most likely came from the UNHCR four-wheel drive vehicle that we saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. Now I think we'll go to 24.43 on the same video. Again, this is all scenes that you were shown yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Now, firstly, are you able to tell us -- and obviously there's a time written on the screen, but first of all, are you able to say whether that is in fact the date, whether this was properly synchronised, this footage, or whether it's of some other date?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can do all types of things with videos, so, no, I cannot confirm or deny whether this is the actual date of that picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can you say where it is?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is obviously in Eastern Bosnia, because I recognise Zele, who is in the front of the picture. Whether he's in Tuzla or whether he's in Srebrenica, I can't confirm it just from this picture that I'm looking at right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I think you mean Senad.

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, Senad.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You said yesterday when shown this -- actually, I'll just find the part of the transcript. It was at page 107, lines 24 to 25, I think, if I could just have a moment. Yes. You say you noticed that there was a wide variety of military uniforms in the group. It's not uniform. And there's that interesting oxymoron of different uniforms. It's correct, isn't it, for a military organisation, that the uniform has to be the same by definition?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only people in my experience who are professional military who have motley uniforms are special ops-type guys just because of the characteristics of their activities, and that's by purpose, not by necessity. In this case, it's by necessity.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So you would agree that different uniforms, as a uniform, is a contradiction in terms?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, particularly for a paramilitary-type group.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, if we go to 27.13.7 on the same video, you were asked about an individual. And again, we won't mention his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: There, who we see in the white hat. I simply want to ask you this: Were you aware whether he was in Srebrenica after you left, later in 1993 or in 1994 or in 1995?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So are you able to say for this footage positively when this was filmed; in what year, and again, aside from what may be indicated on the scene?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a historical fact that I know General Morillon made his first trip into the Srebrenica pocket to Cerska and that this individual accompanied him on that trip.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We don't see General Morillon in that picture, do we?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we do not, and I do not know who the other individual in blue is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now we're going to go to 46.57 on the same video.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, first I want you to look at the surrounding scenery and -- as this plays and tell us whether this is in fact in Srebrenica. And I mean the town when I say that.

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That looks very similar to the terrain I knew in Srebrenica. It would be on the northern part of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is it anywhere near the PTT building?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stop. Go back three -- about three frames, please. I need to look at the hills in the back left side.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Stop. No, it doesn't appear to be directly by the PTT building. It actually appears to be further north, more towards the soccer fields, looking at that location. I didn't see any -- I didn't see the hospital or the PTT building or some of the other key large buildings I was familiar with. This valley area looks too open, also. Downtown Srebrenica is a much tighter environment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Now, you were asked yesterday -- you were shown this video and you were asked questions about it in relation to the incident of General Morillon being kept, initially against his will, in Srebrenica. It was put to you, and it's at page 120, line 1, it was asked whether seeing this video changed your mind, whether there might have been authorities involved in the taking or holding people in abeyance at the PTT building on the 11th of March when you arrived. Did you understand from that question that this video was supposed to be in Srebrenica, in the town?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did that mislead you or confuse you?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the key comment on this one --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have an objection, because that was -- not a question was asked by the Prosecution and so one cannot be misled by what was not asked, and I'm now wondering is the witness being misled by this series of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That seems a rather sort of tit-for-tat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones, I think we can move to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think the witness has clearly stated that he was. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, one point when being shown this video I think you referred to a charismatic -- indications of a charismatic leader because people were applauding. Were you saying that you can conclude from a few people applauding that one is in the presence of a charismatic leader, or were you saying something else?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm going to rephrase your question. Based on what I saw on that video and the reaction of the crowd to that personality, it was very positive, not negative. They were giving him due respect and attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want to ask you about this book by Larry Hollingworth. In preparing for testifying, I asked you, did I not, to read a couple of chapters from that book?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And now you told us yesterday that Mr. Hollingworth was not a trained military observer. Correct?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In what you read in his book, was it all a hundred per cent accurate or was there any exaggeration or artistic license or any matters that you didn't entirely agree with?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as getting this general flow of the event, he got that right; but with the details, he elaborated or added or subtracted to it. He didn't keep a journal, and therefore his particulars were not exactly accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Brydensholt, do you have any questions? Judge Eser?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Yes, I have two short points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Mr. Dudley, when -- you put some weight on this C3I environments and it seemed to be used as a yardstick for assessing the efficiency of an army, and so on. Now, my question is: When you make reference to CIA -- C3I, I'm sorry -- you see I'm not a military man.

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: If you make reference to this, did you mean it as a description of reality which, apart from the present situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, would be common to all normal armies, armies all over the world, or would you use -- make reference to these requirements in terms of a proposition, how an army ideally be -- should be?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to take a few minutes to answer that question. First off, as a trained military observer, I am equipped with various yardsticks to measure the capabilities of various armed forces I meet in the field. For C3I or command, control, communications, and intelligence, these are key tools that any commander would need to be an effective commander in the field. There's various ways and means to accomplish those four criteria, but if one or more of them are missing, then the commander becomes quickly handicapped in his ability to lead and accomplish specific missions, particularly combined-arms operations. And that's what I was judging.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Thank you. Another question is the following: If I -- if my recollection is correct, you did not meet Naser. Now, did you meet any other group leaders while you have been in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I vaguely met a few group leaders. One instance when the first time I went up to do a satellite shot just south of Srebrenica, the dilapidated vehicle we were riding in broke down. A group of fighters were coming back down the hill on this cart being pulled by an old tractor, and they offered us a ride and we took it. I used that opportunity to ask some very, very simple questions because all they spoke was Bosniak. That's how I met different group leaders; in that type of informal environment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, when you characterised Naser Oric as the first among equals, now is this your own assessment or was it also reported to you by others in these terms?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my own assessment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Judge Eser. And I thank you, Colonel Dudley. This basically means that your testimony ends here. Madam Usher will escort you out from the courtroom pretty soon, but before you leave us, may I, on behalf of Judge Brydensholt, Judge Eser, also on behalf of the Tribunal, thank you for having come over to give testimony here. And I'm sorry if you had to overstay beyond what we had anticipated. I also wish to take this opportunity, Madam Schildge, to thank -- ask you to thank the ambassador, US ambassador, for the cooperation extended to the Tribunal and to the parties, both Defence and Prosecution. We appreciate that very much, and if you could on our behalf extend our best wishes, seasonal wishes, to him and the rest of the embassy staff. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It was my privilege.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We also wish you a safe journey back home, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So now we get the next one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Birtley, welcome to this Tribunal. Very soon you are going to start giving evidence. I don't know if it's your first time here in this Tribunal in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I'll explain very briefly what the procedure is. The procedure is that you are required, first and foremost, to make a solemn declaration equivalent to an oath in several domestic jurisdictions, that in the course of your testimony you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. After which you will then be asked a series of questions by Mr. Jones, who is co-counsel in the Defence team for Mr. Oric, who is the accused. And Mr. Jones will then be followed by Mr. Wubben, who is the lead counsel for the Prosecution in this case. It is my understanding, at least, that the two parties have cooperated and agreed amongst themselves that they will do their utmost to finish with your testimony today, and that would make it possible for you to leave immediately after. So please take the solemn declaration text in your hand, read it out, and that will be your undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, sir. Please make yourself comfortable, and we'll take off straight away. Mr. Jones, please allow a small interval, small pause between question and answer, because whatever is said here -- you both speak the same language and that needs to be interpreted into French and into Bosnian. So please take consideration -- take that into consideration. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Good morning from me firstly, Mr. Birtley.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, please give your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Anthony John Birtley.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you were born on the 29th of June, 1955, in Germany?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm going to be pausing for the interpretation so -- just so your know. And your nationality is British?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you're a journalist by professional, and specifically a war reporter?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: How long have you worked as a war reporter?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: 15 or 16 years now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And have you covered wars in Lebanon, Iran, Iraq, Chechnya, Somalia, Rwanda, Sudan, Cambodia, Sri Lanka, among other places?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, did you go to Sarajevo in July, 1992, to cover the war in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you stay in Sarajevo for the rest of 1992 and part of early 1993?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, apart from a couple of trips out towards Mostar, but basically most of the time in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, when you were in Sarajevo in that period, did you hear anything about the situation in Eastern Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes. There was humanitarian reports from the United Nations about the worsening situation in Eastern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And while you were in Sarajevo, did you ever hear the name of Naser Oric in relation to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You need to answer yes or no because it didn't --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No [Realtime transcript read in error "I did"].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see in the transcript "I did." Now it's gone, all right, that's perfect, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And in fact when you were in Sarajevo, were you given the name of someone who was commander in Srebrenica who was not Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: I was given the name of somebody I thought was the commander that I should look for when I got into Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And was that the name Naser Oric or someone else?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: No, it wasn't; someone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, did you at some stage go to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Because as it is, the transcript could be misleading. I understood the witness to say, no, it wasn't Naser Oric, it was someone else. But as it is, the transcript says, No, it wasn't someone else. Did I interpret your answer correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You did, yes. No, it wasn't Naser Oric. It was someone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Birtley.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If -- we are having a few problems because some of the interpreters are not hearing you properly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll move closer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you could move closer to the microphones, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you at some stage go to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: I did in 1993; March 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you know when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Somewhere around the 8th or 9th of March. I can't be exact.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And how did you reach the enclave?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: I was flown in a Bosnian army helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And what type of helicopter was that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: It was an MI8, Russian-built helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was that a new or old --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Pretty old.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And was yours the only helicopter that went in or were there others?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: There were two helicopters going that day. I didn't know at the time where the second one was going but I learned afterwards it was going to Konjevic Polje. The one I was on went to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And what happened to the one which was going to Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: I learnt later it crashed. It was brought down by fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And were you trying to get into Srebrenica for some time before you actually arrived there?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes. I spent something like three weeks trying to work a way in. Originally, I was going to go in by foot with a unit of Bosnian soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you travel into Srebrenica with anyone else?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: There was a Bosnian man called Haris Nezirovic who was a journalist who came along and acted as my interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Three and a half weeks, I think it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: What caused you to leave?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: I was wounded. I suffered a bad injury to my leg, and the United Nations flew me out for treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And was that the only time you were injured while you were in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: No. I had two smaller wounds before that. Nothing serious, but just slight wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But from what? What caused those wounds?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Shrapnel from mortar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And do you recall on what day you were wounded?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: The -- which time? Which wound?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The one which led to you leaving, the serious wound?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yeah, I think it was April the 3rd at 10.30. I know that because my daughter was being christened at 11.30 in Cyprus at the time, so a very relevant time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And when you arrived in Srebrenica, where did you stay?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: The first night I stayed with someone who was described to me as a police officer, with him and his wife. And after that, then I moved to a hotel called the Domavija Hotel, which was under the command of one fighter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And why did you go there, to the Domavija Hotel?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: My recollection is that normally when I go into these situations I try and find someone who's happy to have me along and somewhere where there's action. And at that time I was told the action was in this particular area which was commanded by the fighter I went with, Hakija.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And do you recall Hakija's last name?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Meholjic, I think, or something like that. I'm not very good on names, but I always remember Hakija. He was a very striking character.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And apart from Hakija and any fighters and yourself, was anyone else staying in the Domavija Hotel?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Not to my recollection, basically fighters and us, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you know someone called Dr. Nedret Mujkanovic?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you know where he was staying in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: He was staying in the Domavija also.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And when you arrived in Srebrenica, were there any other internationals already there?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: There was one German photographer, Philipp von Recklinghausen.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you know how he got into Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: I understand he walked from Tuzla via Cerska, when that was still open. And later on, the Serbs took Cerska and that route was not possible anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would ask if the witness can be shown 872, D872.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, firstly I'd ask whether you recognise any people on -- in this scene.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes, the one on the left is I think Major Dudley. The guy on the right is Senad, who is a young Bosnian guy I came across a lot. And one -- I can't remember his name, but he was part of what was called the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know whether Senad ever performed any function for Philipp?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: I think he helped with translation. Philipp didn't have any knowledge of Bosnian and Senad had lived in Germany and spoke German, so he was acting like a translator for him sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did Senad act as a translator or interpreter for Philipp only or also for other people?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: No, I saw that when the UN came in with General Morillon, which was a couple days after I arrived, Senad was being used as a translator for them also.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, did you film scenes in Srebrenica while you were there?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And what sort of camera did you use?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: A very basic Sony Video 8. I had two cameras, one with the night capability, and that was specifically for the aid drops that were being done at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And so, are the -- I think what's called the rushes, are they in that system, in the Sony Video 8 system?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In filming these scenes, did you go out and about in Srebrenica and in the surrounding area?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: I did, every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And can you explain a bit about what exactly that entailed and what you were concerned with filming?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: At that time the -- there was a lot of military activity. Serbs were pushing, and there was lots of refugees fleeing their villages, so there were constant streams of people on the roads and the tracks, carrying their belongings, whatever they could actually get away with. And they were streaming into Srebrenica. So I would go out to the furthest point I could and film them and speak to them about what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you ever go out and about with Hakija?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And was what you filmed broadcast to the outside world?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, please allow a little -- a short pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And via what network was that broadcast?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Ostensibly by ABC News in America but also in Britain through the BBC and ITN, and then that went all around the world then.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did that have any impact on events in Srebrenica, the broadcasting of your reports?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes, it did. It -- well, I learnt basically from the UN on the ground and also from listening to the BBC that there was a great more impetus for the international community to get involved in what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And was General Morillon's presence also contributing to that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes, it was. A combination of my video and his stand, deciding to stay in Srebrenica, really highlighted the plight of the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And do you have any opinion or did you have any opinion as to what would have happened without those two events?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: It seemed to me that -- and also kind of the military observers from the UN, that I think Srebrenica would have fallen fairly soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And is that something which the people in Srebrenica feared or not at the time?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes, they were very, very frightened. It was a time of chaos and panic, and people were fearing the worst.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, without mentioning any names, how did you actually get your film out to the outside world?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Basically, the UN -- I mean, the first tape was taken out by people who came in with General Morillon, and after that, tapes were out with UN trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And was that an easy or a difficult business, getting your tapes out?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: It became easy, but it was difficult in the beginning because the Serbs were looking for the tapes. After the first tape came out and the first reports were aired, they were then looking for them. And they actually captured one of my tapes that was being taken out by an aid worker. So after that, we had to use more careful means of getting the tapes out.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you know what was on that captured film?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly, but two things I do remember: One was the first evacuation of women and children on the UN convoy that came in. I remember that graphically because it was very disturbing scenes of people desperately trying to get on the trucks to leave and people actually throwing, physically throwing, their babies and young children on to people in the trucks. And the other was some front line fighting I had covered and filmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So is it right, then, that in fact you observed front line fighting when you were in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And can you describe for us what you saw, what sort of things?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: I was in a trench south-east of Srebrenica towards the Drina River to the Serb territory, and a lot of heavy fire from artillery and mortars came in to the position I was in. And there was one fighter who was killed. I mean, the Bosnian people were firing back as well, but they didn't have mortars or anything, they just had guns. I couldn't see what they were firing at, it was too far away.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And do you know how those fighters were getting to the lines?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Some -- some were going by a very small kind of mini-van, but most of them were walking.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And what sort of arrangements were there for how long they would stay on the lines, if you were able to see?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: I don't recall that there were any arrangements. It was done between them, and I didn't speak the language so I didn't really understand, but it seemed, you know, a day, or sometimes more.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I want to ask you a little about any local authorities in Srebrenica. First, were you aware of a mayor?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If the witness could please be shown Exhibit P318 -- sorry, I suppose this is the video exhibit, my apologies. In fact we'll freeze it. Play it from 4.07 to 4.14.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry, it's a bit blurred there, but do you recognise --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The man in the blue?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's who?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: That's the man I understood to be the mayor.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And in fact, do you recognise the man to his right?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And who is that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: He was Zelad, I think. I can't remember his name exactly, but he was one of the -- he had one arm. He lost his arm and he was a member of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned a War Presidency in Srebrenica, so you were aware of that as a local authority?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was the War Presidency doing anything to help refugees as they arrived in the town?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: I can't say they were or they were not. I mean, basically I saw in the street nobody helping these people, so I assumed there was nothing in place to help them. I don't know if they'd taken any steps or any measures to help these people because I wasn't present when they were having any of the meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you observe any sort of structure dealing with the refugee situation?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: No, I didn't, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, are you aware of how the local authorities regarded the authorities in Sarajevo? Do you recall any instance in that regard?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: I mean, some people were quite critical. They felt they'd been abandoned by Sarajevo and --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you at one time invoke the name of President Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment before you answer this question. Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Sorry to interrupt, but the question was: "Are you aware of how the local authorities regarded the authorities in Sarajevo?" And then the answer was: "I mean, some people were quite critical." Not pointing out to what extent these people the witness mentioned were indeed local authorities. So I would ask for a clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. Fair enough. When you gave your answer and you said: "I mean, some people were quite critical." These people, did you mean people in authority in Sarajevo or just the ordinary people of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ordinary people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ordinary people. But the question -- not Sarajevo, sorry, of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ordinary people. But the question referred to the authorities in Srebrenica. Have you got a clue as to how they viewed -- they regarded the authorities in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't get any sense from these people, but I was basically with Hakija and he was very expressive and had many opinions on many things, including that, and he wasn't very happy with Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes can go back to that question if you want to, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just one small follow-up on that. Did you at any time invoke the name of President Izetbegovic as a reason for you being allowed to leave, and receive a response?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Yes. President Izetbegovic started the process whereby I was able to go to Srebrenica. And when I was there and after ten or 12 days I really wanted to leave and I said, Well, Izetbegovic said I could leave when I wanted, and there was general laughter and hilarity at this, and somebody said basically: Who the hell is he here? And I got the message quite clear that that didn't mean anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you told us that during the time that you were in Srebrenica there was essentially a Serb offensive. Would that be fair to say?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was the defence of the Srebrenica pocket organised in any way that you could see?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: To a certain extent, yes, I think it was. People from their various areas would go and defend, be on front lines. To what extent that extended all around the pocket, I don't know, because I didn't visit the whole area. But also there was a tremendous lack of organisation that appeared to me from people who were -- you know, were in danger of being overrun by the Serbs. I mean, there were no anti-tank defences, roads were empty and open and free for tanks to move down. I thought it looked a pretty desperate situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, you told us how you stayed at the Hotel Domavija and I want to go back to that for a moment. How long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: During my entire stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you get to know Hakija Meholjic?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: As well as you can do when you don't speak the language, yes. But I drank with him sometimes and we had conversations where if Haris Nezirovic, the translator, was there, then I could participate. If not, I waited for someone else who could speak some broken English.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And what sort of character did he have?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Larger than life. Very strong person. Stubborn, opinionated, with some likable qualities.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And in physical appearance, was he bearded or clean-shaven?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Bearded.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was that common or uncommon at the time in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: It was pretty common, actually, because I don't think there were any razors, and myself, I mean, I grew a beard while I was there as well because there was no water and there was no razors. When I first met Hakija he looked like what I thought the Bosnians called Chetniks, very bearded, very rugged looking. I was quite surprised to find out he was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did he ever say anything about when he would cut his beard?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: When there was peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you ever see him having cut his beard?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes. I went back to Srebrenica about seven months after I left, when I recovered and I could walk again. And I went back to Srebrenica and Hakija had shaved his beard off. He thought it was peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, as far as the Hotel Domavija is concerned when you were there in March 1993, did other fighters stay in that hotel?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: What were the conditions like there?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Well, I think compared to some of the conditions refugees were living in, they were quite good. But, you know, my first impression was they were pretty horrible. Basic conditions, windows blown in, damage from shells, and the toilets were horrible. No running water, of course, no electricity.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Staying in that hotel in the evenings without electricity and with people with the appearance you described, if I may, people having beards, was it easy to distinguish between people among the faces you would see?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Well, I mean Hakija, you would never mistake Hakija, you would never mistake Nedret, the doctor, and one or two other people. But a lot of -- there was so many people coming in and out, it's very difficult to keep track. And it was -- I couldn't pick out everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, how were the fighters in the Hotel Domavija referred to, if they were referred to?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: It was always told to me by Haris that these were Hakija's men. It was always Hakija's men. Or you're going to go with Hakija's men. Or Hakija says you can go with his guys. Generally, "Hakija's men" was the term.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you told us you went to the lines, I think, with Hakija's men. Can you tell us whether each fighter had his own rifle at the lines, or how that worked.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: No. Generally, they didn't have -- not everybody had their own weapon. They would go -- basically, it's like a shift. So the outgoing shift would give their weapon to the guy who was coming in.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you hear of Naser Oric when you were in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And first of all, dealing with Hakija and his men. What did you hear about Naser from Hakija, from Hakija specifically?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Well, Hakija was not really impressed with Naser. He said he was a brave guy but didn't have a military brain, and he was not -- I mean, Hakija was his own man, and I think kind of -- he wanted to put over the impression to me that he was really in control of his own thing and he didn't really rate Naser as a military commander, basically.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you ever ask Hakija whether Naser was Hakija's boss or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: I think it came up in conversation once which, you know -- actually, I think I referred to something and Hakija laughed about, certainly not my boss. I think he's quite expletive, actually, in terms of the colourful way that Bosnians can be, in swearing about Naser.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So just to clarify that, you made some reference and Hakija laughed at the suggestion that Naser was his boss?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah. I mean, nothing could be further from the truth as far as Hakija was concerned, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you ever speak to Dr. Nedret Mujkanovic on this subject?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And what was his opinion?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Pretty much the same, but he was not so -- so strong in his condonation of Naser's abilities. He was a bit more liberal in the way he explained it. You know, very impressed with Naser being a brave man, but also mindful of the fact that he didn't have that kind of military brain that could work and save them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Dealing with Nedret now, Dr. Mujkanovic, how was he regarded by the Srebrenica, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: As a legend. And he's pretty highly regarded by me as well because I think he saved my leg. So he's certainly a legend for me well. Everywhere you went, they would call him a legend and they were grateful, because he did an absolutely fantastic job there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We have a new exhibit which we'd like to pass up. It's a newspaper article of Peter Mass: "Binding up the wounds, Bosnian surgeon recounts life under siege," Washington Post April 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Firstly, if you can confirm whether or not you saw this when you were here in The Hague with us.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And I'm just going to look at two short passages. It starts at the top: "Tuzla Bosnia. Nedret Mujkanovic is a physician who specialises in medieval medical practices but not by choice." If we drop down, referring to Srebrenica, it says: "There he conducted more than 200 operations without anaesthesia, including amputations." It goes on to describe that in a bit more detail, and then I think it's the sixth paragraph -- fifth paragraph: "The situation was brutally simple. As Serb nationalist forces tighten there siege on Srebrenica, medical supplies from the outside were cut off along with electricity and running water. Soon there was no medical equipment and no medicine, not even aspirin. Mujkanovic's principal tools were his eyes, his hands, a stethoscope and a few scalpels." I just want to ask whether that reflects the experience that you had as well, what you saw, or not?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If we turn to page 3, I think there's a reference to you there. "One of Mujkanovic's friends in Srebrenica was Tony Birtley, an ABC news correspondent who sneaked into the city and was able to transmit to the world the horror of what was happening there. Birtley suffered a shrapnel wound to his leg a month ago and before Mujkanovic operated on him, he squeezed the surgeon's hand and asked him not to amputate. Knowing Mujkanovic was a smoker in a city where cigarettes are scarcer than smiles, Birtley joked that he would find a carton of Marlboros for the doctor if the leg was saved." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: He did, and he got two cartons of Marlboro for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would ask for an exhibit number for this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, what's the next D99 --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D999, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So this document, which consists of four pages, containing an article called "Binding up the wounds, Bosnian surgeon recounts life under siege" is being tendered and marked as Exhibit D999. We are almost there. It's one more and we'll make it 1.000, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. That's our plan, to get to D1000 today.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you ever see Naser Oric at the Hotel Domavija when you stayed there?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, were you aware of any sort of police force in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: I mean, people were referred to as policemen, and the only kind of evidence I saw of that was on the day of an evacuation when people with guns were in charge of organising the evacuation. But they were not wearing uniforms or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you say they were in charge of organising the evacuation. Did they manage to organise it or keep control?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: They did not keep control. It was complete and utter chaos, and some of them were firing in the air to try and control people, pulling people back, pushing them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, we're going to look at some video footage and just for you to confirm whether or not you saw it, but that would be better after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In fact, I think -- yes, if we could take the break now that would be best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So how are we for time? Are you on schedule, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm about halfway through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that should be right. Am I correct or not, Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Halfway through, I don't know, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's have a break of 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Birtley, were going to look at some video footage and I'll just ask you to tell us whether or not you shot it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And it's D700, the exhibit, and we can start with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: "Arriving at a village near Srebrenica just to be totally engulfed by" --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We're going to start it again so we get the sound track right from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: "My first recollection is arriving at a village near Srebrenica just to the totally engulfed by hundreds and hundreds of people. I felt I was standing in a movie, and I kept expecting someone to say 'Cut' and I saw all these people with these gaunt, haunted faces and they've all got expressions, it's like life was drained out of them. Life was ebbing away. There was very little caring by the so-called authorities for new arrivals. Nobody cared for the refugees. They were left for days on the street. No one cared anything about them. They arrived, we followed a family through, and they had been walking for something like 17 hours. You know, the mother carrying the little boy who had been wounded by shrapnel in the hand. He had been wounded at the same time as his father. They came. They didn't know where they were going, they had no relatives or friends. "Where does this man recommend they can sleep? Where does this man recommend they can go? "I don't know where. This town has 60.000 refugees and there's only room for 10.000. Have you seen how many people are sleeping on the street? "We helped them carry the sacks. It was a very, very small gesture but this woman was toiling under two great sacks, and I must admit, I found one sack very difficult, but she had two of them. It struck me that I can't believe that these people were people and they didn't want to know --"

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think we can stop there. We don't need to see the whole video.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Firstly, can you confirm that it was you who we saw?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you recall these refugees arriving?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Those images will stay with me for life.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And was there in fact anyone helping them find accommodation or was that something you in fact helped her with?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: This particular lady, I did in fact help her find a room in an office building, but I didn't see any signs of anyone else actually from Srebrenica helping anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And as far as what's recorded in what we've just seen, was that the situation as you recall it, the descriptions of life ebbing out and people's faces, their gaunt faces, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. A sense of hopelessness and fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We're going to play another section now. Just -- I think it's a minute and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: "I think in Eastern Bosnia to be a Bosnian soldier you've got to be resigned to defeat. You've got to be resigned to injury, and also you've got to be resigned to death. It's a total mismatch. It was a big fight, the equivalent of Mike Tyson fighting some 15-year-old with both arms tied behind his back. They simply do not have weapons to compete on a level footing with what the Serbs have got. They have 1948, 1950 rifles, they have Kalashnikovs if they're lucky. They've got a couple of tanks they captured from the Serbs but they can't fire them because they ran out of ammunition a long, long time ago. In my latter days in Srebrenica, I went to the funeral of a soldier, which -- they are very common because soldiers are being killed all the time, but it was significant because he had been killed when there was a so-called cease-fire. Everybody said there was a cease-fire. "And similarly, we had the funeral of this 22-year-old young man whose head had been blown off. There was a typical scene of his brother sobbing uncontrollably, distraught with grief, the father trying to hang on to his emotions, to have some kind of semblance of dignity. He sat there for a few seconds, and held the hand of his son, his eyes welling up with tears."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you recall filming those scenes?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Firstly, as far as the fighters in Srebrenica were concerned, did they appear as we saw them on this video?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No or very few uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Very few uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And the weapons, as you described?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes, exactly that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In fact, I think following on from that section that we saw, you go on and say how you then went to the lines and that was where you injured. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
