utterances.text: And we won't -- in the interests of time, we won't play that section now. We'll play a very brief few sections of another part of this tape, and that should conclude it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: "Tony Birtley, set the stage for us. What is it we're going to see and hear next? "I think we're going to see one of the scenes that will stay with me, and I think for the people who saw the video, for many, many, many years, and that is the sight of complete and utter desperation of people who simply want to get out of a situation and are prepared to do anything to do that. "I couldn't believe what I was seeing. I think sometimes in journalism we can be wont to steer towards hyperbole but there's nothing you could say to really describe what was going on, the sheer panic and the desperation of those people."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And again, that's scenes which you filmed?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier that you also filmed evacuation scenes on tapes which were captured by the Serbs. Would that be different scenes from these, then?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Fairly similar scenes, although the desperation was captured on the camera in terms of babies actually being thrown physically into the trucks. That's what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, besides the footage we've seen which was broadcast, did you film a great deal more footage?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes. I filmed -- I don't know how much was broadcast in the end, but I filmed something about ten or 11 hours of material.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And among that footage, did you recall interviews with some of the internationals who were in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And would that include Major Rex Dudley?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: A Canadian soldier called Donny Paris?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Some of the Bosnian doctors working in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: A Canadian soldier called McAllister?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'd like to go to private session just for the next name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session for a short while, please. [Private session].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We saw on this tape that you were interviewed by Cokie Roberts while you were still in Srebrenica. Can you tell us how that was arranged.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: That was by the only means you could get communication, that was by ham radio from the PTT building in Srebrenica, and then that was patched through to Sarajevo and then connected by phone to New York.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In fact, I think I should say that Cokie Roberts appears in one part of the tape but not the bit we saw. Nothing turns on it. Do you know who operated that ham radio?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: The -- there was a guy, I always remember his name because I saw him later, Ibrahim Becirovic, and then there were twins and I can't remember their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If the witness could please be shown D785.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If you could look at that photograph and tell us whether you recognise the people there.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes, they are the twins.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And was that the set-up, the ham radio set-up which you saw?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: That looks -- that's the ham radio. When I was there, there was a bigger table, and that thing which looks like a Morse code thing, I didn't remember -- I don't remember seeing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Apart from the ham radio, was there any other way for you to communicate with the outside world?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did Serbs intercept your communications on the ham radio, actually interrupt?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yeah, frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Just to clarify one matter. You mentioned Ibrahim Becirovic earlier and then the twins. Were they in different locations or in the same location?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: In the same location. They took it in turns to operate the radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And what would happen when the Serbs would interrupt on the communications?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: They would then change frequency and try and find another one. It sometimes took five or ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Were the Serbs aware of your presence in Srebrenica at that time?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yeah, they gave me a few messages, so they knew of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: What sort of messages?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Well, of course this was translated to me by Haris, but basically that they're going to come and kill everybody and they were going to kill me last. And just general things like what they would do to my mother and things.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, going back to this room, was there any sort of guard barring entrance to this room?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If someone were to say that the ham radio consisted of a big, solid, commercial, 3-metres-by-3-metres object with many switches and knobs, which was a serious piece of machinery, what would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: No, that was it. It was a very small box. I think there could be confusion because in the PTT building there was telephone equipment, which was completely rendered useless because of the war and there was no phone lines. So I seem to remember there was equipment, but this was definitely the only thing they used.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, finally I'm moving to a -- well, two more topics. Do you remember being present when a Serb prisoner or detainee was released?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you film at least part of that scene?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And do you remember how you came to be at the scene, the handover?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly. There was so much going on and I think I came across it by accident or I was told, but I can't say with any degree of honesty.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was General Morillon -- well, I want to deal with this in the following way. Perhaps it would help actually if you could have the photograph D997. Did you film -- were you actually filming this scene?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And is this the -- at least a still from that scene?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: It looks like it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can you identify any of the people we see there?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: To the left we see one of the Canadian UN guys, Sergeant Morrison. I remember him because I had a lot to do with him. It looks like Rex Dudley to the right, and then I don't know who the other one is kneeling down.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And can you see the Serb prisoner anywhere in that picture?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: I can see him basically next to Sergeant Morrison. It's like as if they are just going to put him on the stretcher.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you know where this was, where this took place?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: I can tell by the building that it was near the municipality, but you know, I couldn't -- I probably couldn't pick out the road today. But that -- there is a very distinctive building, the municipality building.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And at this location where the prisoner was -- I think we can see or perhaps you said was being placed on the stretcher, was General Morillon present?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: No, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you recall who performed translation for General Morillon?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: There was a Serb-speaking UN guy with a Slavic name. I can't remember exactly his name, but he was with Morillon all the time. I could recognise him, but I can't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And was he present at this scene?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: To my recollection, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you ever see him apart from General Morillon?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you've told us -- well, firstly, did you ever see Naser Oric in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you recall whether he was present at this handover?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: I don't recall him being there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And if the witness could please be shown Exhibit D998, please. I wonder if I might be permitted to lead the name of General Morillon's interpreter. I don't know if it's a matter in dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't have any problems unless the Prosecution has.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I don't have any problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would you recognise the interpreter for General Morillon as being Mr. Mihailov?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, if you look at this photograph, do you know where this was taken?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: This is him when he's on the stretcher. I think it's inside the APC that they were taking him to the Serb side in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you, in fact, film this prisoner inside the APC?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: How close were you to him?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: I was sitting on top of the APC, looking in. I mean, a few feet, and then -- I think that's the closest I got.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Were there any signs on the face of the -- of this man whether he'd been beaten? By that I mean any blood or bruising or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: No. I could only see his face, but he looked extremely gaunt and weak, but I didn't see any signs of beating.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did he have any bandages on his face?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I think you've said: "Yes, he looked extremely gaunt and weak." What, if anything, did appear to be wrong with this man?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: I remember he had extreme difficulty in walking and it seemed to me that he was shielding his eyes from the light. So I drew the conclusion, either wrongly or rightly, that he had been in a darkened room for some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you see during your time in Srebrenica, or not, people who were as thin as him?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: I saw a lot of very, very thin people. Yeah, some extremely thin people, but I'm not sure as thin as him, but pretty thin.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Where was this man taken in the APC, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: He was being taken to Bratunac, which was the Serb line of control, and -- but I got out of the APC before then because I didn't think -- and in fact General Morillon didn't think it was wise for me to go to the Serb side because they were not very happy with me, so I got out before.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When you say "General Morillon didn't think it was wise" for you to go to the Serb side, was he actually travelling in the APC or was this general advice?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: General advice.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So in fact, as you were travelling from the place where we saw the first photograph towards Bratunac, was General Morillon or his assistant in the APC?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: No, they were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: One question on this: As far as the footage from which this photograph came, have you actually provided that or not to us --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I have two -- finished with those photographs. I have two last areas which I can cover very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Firstly, I would be grateful if the witness could be shown -- it's a video P427, and if we could start around 47.06. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I want to ask you to look at this and see if you can recognise where this was filmed or, in any event, whether it is in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: No, that's not Srebrenica -- well, not the time that I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Well, first of all, there's a big open space, and there was no open spaces in Srebrenica like that, certainly no safe ones. And I can tell by the UN soldier - who I don't know who that is - he was not in Srebrenica when I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm finished with that exhibit. Now, finally there's one last exhibit I would like to hand up, and it's the ERN numbers 03731116 to 03731117. And while it's being handed around, it's Republika Srpska, Ministry of the Interior, state security service centre, Sarajevo, dated 15 January 1994, Official Note. Subject: Stay of APC crews in the territory of Republika Srpska. Now, firstly, did we review this document with you when you came to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm just going to read two sections. It starts off: "Upon finding out that an ABC crew, consisting of journalist Antony John Birtlax and translator Andrea Pavletic intend to come to our territory and record several TV clips, given that they are in anti-Serb mood, an informative interview was made with translator Dragana Jovanovic from Belgrade, in order to collect more complete information about the activities of this crew." Are you familiar with Andrea Pavletic and Dragana Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Well, I'm married to Andrea Pavletic, so I know her quite well. And Dragana was the ABC helper in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If we turn to the second page, it says: "According to earlier findings, journalist Anthony Birtley has an extremely anti-Serb attitude and in his reports from Sarajevo he talked about Serbs and Serbian fighting in an insulting and false manner on several occasions. He is the author of the 'story' of raping Muslim women, the trial of Erak, the blockade of Srebrenica, the suffering of Muslims in Sarajevo, and alike. We think that he should be permanently forbidden from staying and working in the territory of Republika Srpska in the future." Now, firstly, did you in fact cover a story of raping of Muslim women?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And that concerned which camp or what area?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: It was a general story on raping of women. I mean, there was raping going on all over the country, but this one centred on a rape crisis centre based in the town of Zenica, and we interviewed women from various parts of Bosnia who had come to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And is it right, as it appears from this, that as a result of those stories you were permanently forbidden from working in the territory of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yeah, I wasn't allowed ever again.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And in fact, is it right that, finally, that you were named Television Journalist of the Year by the Royal Television Society in Britain because of what you filmed in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would ask for an exhibit number for this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this document, which consists of two pages in Serbo-Croat and two pages in English with ERN 03731116 to 1117, is being tendered and marked as Defence Exhibit D1000.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Jones. Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Please bear me a moment to put the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Birtley.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I will do my best to finish today. It partly depends of you limiting your answers when you can be short, and if you don't know, please respond that. As you are aware, my name is Mr. Wubben; I am lead counsel for the Prosecution. I'll start with my first question. You were in Srebrenica at the time in March 1993, beginning April. You were reporting regarding the humanitarian situation. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: You shot footages of people in the streets, refugees. Did you also interview people in their own houses in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And what did you learn from their situation?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: The most common thing at the time was two things: No food and scared of the Serbs overrunning Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: How did the people in those houses that you interviewed or that you spoke to consider the situation regarding the refugees coming into town?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Well, basically, they were uncomfortable that so many people were in Srebrenica when there was not enough for them, and they were expected more and more to try and make place for their refugees to come and stay with them and there was overcrowding. So there was -- but to be honest, I didn't interview so many people in their own houses in Srebrenica; I was interviewing mainly refugees who had come and left their homes behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Those refugees who entered the city, was that a kind of daily stream or --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: -- every week?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: No, on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: On a daily basis. Did you also learn that prior to your arrival or shortly after your arrival a stream had been increased by the fact of people leaving the villages of Konjevic Polje and Cerska area?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: I had learnt prior to that from UN briefings in Sarajevo that there was a humanitarian problem in Eastern Bosnia, but we didn't know exactly how bad that problem was because nobody was going in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Were you aware of any increasing of this stream of refugees in the weeks prior to your arrival?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: I can't remember that far back, actually. I know there was, you know, reasonable information to make me want to go there. So, I mean, I think it stands to reason that there was information coming out that there was a humanitarian problem there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Apart from a humanitarian problem or perhaps also linked with it, was there also a kind of black market for any shortages of food or medicines to deal with?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: I never heard of that before, and I certainly didn't see any kind of black market in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No dealing with the Serbs, trading goods?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: I never heard of them trading with the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No selling of medicines outside a hospital circuit?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: I never heard that, no. There was not enough medicine to go around, and I think someone would have been strung up and hanged if they had been dealing with the Serbs, quite honestly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I want to show a video, D700. It's the first part of it, two clips. And it should be shown on Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Mr. Birtley, I invite you to take a look at the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: "... parcels land, and surprisingly, the first sign --"

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Sorry. Please stop. Can you please start from the beginning. "We've seen eerie pictures of American planes dropping their bulky beacons of survival. Tonight, we see where the parcels land, and surprisingly, the first sign of an American military man on the ground in Eastern Bosnia. He's witnessed the impact of the air drops. These scenes come to us from the town of Srebrenica, a place almost impossible to get to. ABC's Tony Birtley finally managed it last week in what can only be described as an heroic effort to let us see what's happening in Srebrenica. Tony travelled by foot and by horseback to get into the isolated area. Since he arrived, he's run out of food and been injured by Serbian fire. But still he smuggled out the story." Yes, please the second part of it, the subsequent part.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: "American planes have successfully air dropped aid into this area for the last five nights running. The villagers say they received only one prepared lunch packet, the rest has been taken by the army."

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Do you recall this clip, this video clip?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Do you recall that you were reporting from your observations regarding an air-dropping?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: No, from that particular report I was reporting what people told me, not my observations. I said "people told me."

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And people were updating you of -- on the outcome of the air-drop, that's what your testimony is?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: My question is: People were giving you information of the functioning of the air drop, whether it was successful or not?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And what did they tell you?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: These people -- this was -- I remember this quite clearly. This was the first day of my arrival, and this was on my way to Srebrenica, so it was a few kilometres away from the centre, and they were telling me about the air drops. I mean -- I later went to see, myself, the air drops in progress, night-time drops. But at that time, it was just what they told me. So people talked a lot about the air drops when they were there because it was very important for them. It was the only way they were getting food.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I surely will understand that, but my question is also related to the content of your reporting. So you were telling you learned from the people you met and what was meant by the "the rest was taken by the army."

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: That's what they told me at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: But did you corroborate what they told you or did you ask any further?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: At that time there, there was no one to ask. And on the--

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Well, the people would provide you with the information, of course.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Well, they were telling me that, so that's their corroboration. I didn't have an official I could turn to at that point and say: Is this true? I asked several people, if I remember rightly, and they told me that they were getting this one lunch packet and the rest was being taken by the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: By soldiers. So is it the army or soldiers or both?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: When I use -- I think I was basically elevating the Bosnians. "Army" is a generic term. You can use "fighters," "militiamen," whatever. This certainly wasn't an army. They were a group of men, as you see from the video before, improperly dressed with poor weapons. They are not an army. They were, you know, defenders, militiamen, whatever. The food -- I was quite convinced later on what I saw, that they were taking some of the food from the air drops.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: But you reported it, believing it to be reliable information to be broadcasted?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: I reported in that report, saying "the people said." So that's not me saying it; I said "the people said."

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: You stated that there were militiamen, local groups. And you also gave testimony regarding Hakija's men. Did you yourself observe in Srebrenica at the time other groups or units than referred to Hakija Meholjic only?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: I was basically all the time with Hakija's men.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: But the question was: Did you observe the existence of other groups or units?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: I saw other groups in the town, but I don't know if they were actually Hakija's men. I don't still remember how many men Hakija had. So if you saw a group of men going on a truck, I couldn't say at that particular point that they were Hakija's men or not. I only knew when I went to the front line that that was his area of control.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: The area of control for Hakija Meholjic was somewhere at the front line?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Well, the whole -- all the way around Srebrenica was the front line. You didn't -- you had to walk a couple of kilometres, and less than that in certain circumstances, and you would come to the front line because Srebrenica was completely surrounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: But my question related to your comment of the area of responsibility or the place to go for by Hakija's men, and you referred to the front line. My question was: Was that a specific tasking or can you clarify that further?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: What was the task of Hakija's men being situated in the Domavija Hotel?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: I mean, their task was to cover the front lines to the south-east towards Serbia, the Bajina Basta and the Drina, and that's where I went with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: So can I take it that their actions were not limited to Srebrenica and the town itself but also the area around it?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: To be honest, I don't know what actions they would have in the town, but I just saw them outside of the town, on the front lines, which was the line around Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And when you were at the front lines, did you observe other units than the unit of Hakija Meholjic?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: I don't know if they were his units or not. I just went to his area which I thought was his responsibility. You see, there's no insignia, most of them didn't have uniforms, so you couldn't see, for example, 31 Brigade or 72 Brigade. You know, he guy's wearing a leather jacket and he's in that area, I took it that he was Hakija's man. I was always given a guide who would take me to his area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: When did you visit that area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: The -- I mean, my first visit was on the day after I arrived. I went straight to the front lines that day. I arrived in the evening in Srebrenica, and the following morning I went out with Hakija himself and a group of people to a point where I could observe the Serb positions across the Drina River and then sort of survey the damage and refugees coming back from various places.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And did Hakija point out to you the Serb positions?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And what was the plan?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: What plan?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: The plan of Hakija?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: I'm not sure he actually had a plan. The immediate plan was that we were not going to be spotted by mortar position, but it was pretty far in the distance but we were still within range of mortars. But he had no plan to attack because they didn't have any weapons sufficient to launch an attack on the Serbs, because they had tanks and artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: On what other occasions did you observe any front line, can you tell me, Mr. Birtley.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I went two or three times -- and then also -- actually, I'm just remembering now that I was going to go to Konjevic Polje before it fell, and some of Hakija's men came with me, but Konjevic Polje was the other side of Srebrenica. And that's when I got wounded the first time, so -- or the second time, I can't remember. And then we had to turn back.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Did you also visit the confrontation line from the yellow bridge of Srebrenica towards Caus Mountain?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to show the video P318. One moment, please. I would like to state that it's for me not the matter of the text provided, so not the translation, it's about the pictures shown and comment by the witness there. Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And one moment. For the record, we're starting at 16 minutes 23.1 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Mr. Birtley, do you recognise any weaponry on this footage?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: It looks like a missile.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: What kind of missile?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Surface-to-air missile.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Pardon, please repeat?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: It looks from that, but it's hazy, a surface-to-air missile.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, we are at still 16 minutes, 41 seconds point 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And, Mr. Birtley, do you also recognise one of the persons or more on this picture or earlier?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Not from that -- earlier I recognised Naser.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Naser who?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Oric.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Can you confirm that the army, the soldiers, the Muslim fighters indeed possessed such missiles?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: I knew of one they possessed. I didn't know of anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Please play the second clip. Your Honours, there will be a second clip shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. For the record, the video started rolling at 24 minutes point 41 point 1 and finished at 24 minutes point 50 point 3 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Mr. Birtley, did you saw this clip?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Did I what?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Did you watch the clip?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: This one?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Did you recognise anyone?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: It looks -- it looks like Naser, but it's not very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Naser who?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Naser Oric, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: The weaponry -- may I point out to the tree. Do you recognise this weaponry?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: AK-47s.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. We are at still 24 minutes point 41 seconds point 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Does this picture reflect your memory that Muslim soldiers, Muslim army, or Muslim fighters in fact used these kind of weaponry?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes, this is the standard weapon in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And -- okay. No further questions in that respect. Did you also notice a kind of device in the hands of the person you pointed out as Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: No, I don't see any device.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Can you please play the clip again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: What can you tell me about that device?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: It looks like a hand-held VHF radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Do you know what type it is?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, we are at still 24 minutes point 47 point 2 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Did you notice or observe when you were in Srebrenica the use of such communication type?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: No, I didn't. Srebrenica is so hilly that it's extremely difficult to have that kind of communication. You've got to be up pretty high to use it. Even where I was, I never saw hand-held radios being used. I remember thinking that communication was one of the big problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you also watch the type of uniforms that they were wearing here in the -- in the clip, the video clip?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Do you recognise that as something that reflects your memory at the time you were in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Some had uniforms. Naser had -- Naser Oric had a uniform and some of the men had uniforms, but the overwhelming majority didn't have uniforms. I don't know when this video was taken. To see somebody with a leather jacket and then trousers standing there tells me that it wasn't in a hostile environment. When I was there and the time it was happening before the cease-fire, they were, to my knowledge, not using VHF radios.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you. I will move on to my next issue. So thank you for this. Mr. Birtley, when you were in Srebrenica, were you aware of the existence of any defence staff related to the organised defence of Srebrenica by the Muslims, the Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Something referred to as the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: That's indeed an entity, a body? What I referred to is a staff specifically raised or as a goal founded on the purpose to support any defence of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: I never heard of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: You never heard of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are in cross-examination, Mr. Wubben. You can ask him a direct question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Are you aware that in February there had been a mobilisation ordered by the Muslim defence in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: You haven't seen the outcome of such a mobilisation that might trigger your attention when I speak about it, that a lot of men were called to take up weapons or to help out? There was no talk about it when you arrived. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: I got there in March. I think it was just a given that, you know, the enemy, so to speak, was coming closer and closer. You've got to defend your home. But I wasn't aware that there was a general call-up of everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Are you familiar with a village in the neighbourhood of Srebrenica called Kutlici?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Are you aware that in March 1993 -- and you were there, isn't it, in March 1993?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: It depends which part of March. I didn't get there until the 9th or 10th of March, so if it was before --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I apologise. It's in the second half of March 1993. There was a mobilisation of an entire population of a village in the neighbourhood of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have a request. I have to further organise my cross-examination and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You would like a break now?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes. It would help if we have a break now, and I am certainly in my assurance that we end today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. All right. Now, we have the break now, reconvening in half an hour's time, that would be 12.15. 12.15, okay. And if you need -- if the recorders or the interpreters need a further short break, we will organise that. All right. We'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, and also I appreciated to get more time for the break. I will be short and in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Mr. Birtley, this morning you -- in your testimony you referred to a person called Haris Nezirovic. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And he's a journalist?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And he acted as your interpreter?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Did he also act as the interpreter of Hakija Meholjic?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Not specifically. He was with me and he interpreted between me and Hakija.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And also between you and the locals?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And what was the nationality of Mr. Nezirovic?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: So he didn't like the Serbs, didn't he? Or you don't know?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: I'm trying to remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would rather that you don't generalise on this because I'm pretty sure that in spite of everything that happened, even when it was happening, I think a lot of Bosnians were against the war, a lot of Serbs were against the war, a lot of Croats were against the war, and I think a great majority of them were against the war. So I would rather not characterise this single individual, whoever he is, and say: Therefore, as a Bosnian, he hated -- or he didn't like the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I didn't use the word "hate," but I'll get to my next question. It was information about an opinion, but I withdraw this question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Did you trust him as an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: I did, yes. I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: -- I had no choice.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And was he also trustful as a person, as a journalist?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: I found him a trustful person, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: So you trusted what he told you upon what the locals told him?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: In sum, he was a competent person?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: He was competent. His English was not perfect, but that's the best I had in that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: So is mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment before this goes off the screen. It's line 22 of the previous page where I made that famous speech. It looks like an answer. It's not an answer. It's my contribution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: That depends, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender a document, and it's not on the exhibit list but during the break I already handed it over to the Defence. Would you please put it on the ELMO. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Mr. Birtley, this is a newspaper article extracted from the Internet. It's headed by the wording "Defeated by the battle for food." Can you read?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: It's by Haris Nezirovic, and Haris Nezirovic is a Bosnian journalist working for the weekly newspaper "Slobodna Bosna." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: If you turn the page, you'll find out that by the end it's stated that Haris Nezirovic is a Bosnian journalist working for the weekly newspaper "Slobodna Bosna." He has been in Srebrenica for three weeks. May I turn to the next page. This is in the heading, referring to The Guardian, London, UK. I take it that is a respectable newspaper?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: May I quote in part of it and you might follow. It's referring, in the first paragraph: "The year-old war in east Bosnian Muslim enclaves of Srebrenica." It's referring in this third paragraph. "From last August, the Bosnian army launched direct attacks on Serbian positions and scored considerable successes, despite being outgunned." Two paragraphs subsequently: "They had artillery and tanks. Victories were at the cost of dozens of dead and scores wounded in every battle, but the troops were undeterred. The men kept going a Bosnian army soldier said." And then on the next page. The third paragraph: "The food crisis was compounded by problems of morale and rampant criminality." Now, apart from your testimony on various issues I already addressed, what is your comment about that? Does that refresh your memory that indeed - and I take it that there was criminality, rampant criminality around --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: I had no knowledge and I had no information given to me by anybody, including Haris Nezirovic, who was with me all the time, that there was anything like this happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And in the third line of that paragraph: "Dozens of Bosnian soldiers said the military number two in Srebrenica, a man who had spent 17 years in prison for double murder, used to beat any soldier who requested basic equipment." Do you agree with me that the number two referred to is Zulfo Tursunovic?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: If Zulfo Tursunovic is number two, do you know who is number one?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: I didn't know there was a number two, so how would I know there was a number one?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that number one should be Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I tender this as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The next number, Madam Registrar, please. P --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P616, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this document, which consists of two pages, purportedly an article from The Guardian of the 15th of April, 1993, entitled "Defeated by the battle for food," by Haris Nezirovic, is being tendered and marked as Prosecution Exhibit P616.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour. Thank you, Mr. Birtley.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there re-examination, Mr. Jones? I thank you, Mr. Jones -- Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps just a couple of questions on this article, which is now P616.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you still have that in front of you, Mr. Birtley?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: No, I don't. It's been taken out.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just two things on this article. I'll just read the first paragraph -- first and second paragraph, and then further down. "The year-old war in east Bosnian enclave of Srebrenica has not been a conflict between organised military units but a desperate struggle for food waged with arms and motivated by an instinct for survival." Firstly pausing there, does that accurately reflect the situation as you found it?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Certainly a desperate struggle for survival, but you know, within that there comes some kind of organisation that people tend to defend their areas where they lived. So I would say it was total lack of organisation, but there was a form that people knew where to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When we see further down the Prosecution referred to the section where it says: "'They had artillery and tanks. We were just cannon fodder,' Hekija Meholjic, a Bosnian brigade commander, said of the Serbs." I take it it's clear from that that it was the Serbs who had artillery and tanks, correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you see any contradiction or not between what's said there, a description of Hakija as a brigade commander and what's said in the first paragraph about there not being organised military units?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Well, I mean, Hakija was never described to me as a Bosnian brigade commander. He wasn't given a rank at all. And Haris is the one who told me that, so I'm a bit surprised that he puts this in a story that was written later.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. And just finally, a passage was read to you about a person who used to "beat any soldier who requested basic equipment." The paragraph after that says: "He would put the men in ranks and tell them to go fight, a teenage fighter said. When a soldier asked if there was anything to eat, the vice-commander would take him and beat him black and blue." Then we get to the last paragraph, and it says: "The local command tried to organise the draft but few soldiers take up arms. Why should they? Maybe they will face beatings while their families starve to death." Now, you were asked about whether there was a draft. Does what you read there give rise to any reflections in that regard?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: I knew nothing of anything like this or any examples of people being beaten. So, you know, I saw people on the front lines eating bread. They didn't have much food, that's for sure. But no one did in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Jones. Judge Brydensholt, do you have a question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: When you witnessed this exchange of a prisoner, you didn't remember how you came to be there when that happened. Could there have been more occasions where prisoners were taken by UN for exchange in the time when you were in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: No. That was the only occasion. I didn't know up until that point that there was a Serb prisoner being held, so I think I got the information from the UN.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Okay. Did you ask if there were more prisoners held? Weren't you inquiring a bit about that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BIRTLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I asked after that and was told there was no one else. He was the last, I was told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Eser, do you have any questions? Mr. Birtley, that brings your testimony to an end. So you will -- you're free to go your way. But before you leave this courtroom, I wish to thank you on behalf of Judge Brydensholt, Judge Eser, and also on behalf of the Tribunal in general for having accepted to come over and give testimony in this case. I also wish to take this opportunity to wish you a safe journey to wherever you're going and also convey to you on behalf of my two colleagues all our best wishes for Christmas and the New Year.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will now be escorted by Madam Usher and given all the assistance you require to facilitate your flight arrangements. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Before we finish and exchange greetings, is there anything by way of housekeeping matter that you would like to raise today? None.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I don't believe so, Your Honour. One thing which just occurs to me is that we may perhaps, in the course of tomorrow, take the opportunity to file maybe a Rule 92 bis motion or something like that, but obviously, given that it is the holiday season, we certainly wouldn't expect that to be dealt with within the usual time limits. So we certainly -- if we do submit anything like that, we're not expecting any immediate responses or -- and we wouldn't oppose any application by the Prosecution for an extension of time because we're not going to try and put them in a position where they have to work unnecessarily over the holidays.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Jones. Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I appreciate that offer from the Defence and I certainly would like to use it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, all right, thank you. That will be the case. On our part, we will always have a skeleton staff here working. We are already working on the two pending motions under Rule 90 and also the Republika Srpska documents. I can't promise you that everything will be finalised before we leave or -- but we'll continue working over the holidays on them, and as soon as we have reached agreement, I'll sign the decisions and hopefully they'll be communicated to you well before we reconvene in January. Now, having said that, as far as sittings go, you realise now that for this year we finish here. And we shall reconvene, I think, if my calculations are good, either on the 11th or on the 12th -- on the 12th of January. I said the 11th, because I think the exchange of greetings with Her Majesty, the Queen of the Netherlands, has been shifted from the 11th to the 10th, but I don't think now we can actually change the schedule that we have. On behalf of Judge Brydensholt and Judge Eser, I should like to wish you all, Christians and non-Christians, the very best for the coming season. And also, I wish you the very best for the New Year, which should see the conclusion of this case, hopefully. I wish you good health, first and foremost, happiness, and all that your heart desires. So -- and I hope to see you all again, please God, on the 12th of January, so when we can continue and hopefully start the conclusive part of the Defence case. Okay. I thank you all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 12th day of January, 2006, at 2.15 p.m. 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.35 p.m.,
